doc.title: Charles Lloyd — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Higgins, Hendrix and the spiritual path
title: King Janaka parable and the artist's struggle
summary: Lloyd tells of a man who leaves King Janaka rather than beg from a beggar and reflects that creative lives are hard.

story.theme_name: Late-career reflections: awards, legacy and life lessons
story.community_name: Looking back: no regrets, what it all meant

blocks.x: But if I was trying to go after gold mines, then I would miss the sound of what’s calling me, you understand? It’s like King Janaka - I’ll be quiet after this, I was trying to tell you - this guy knew King Janaka and he went to him and he wanted to borrow some bread. So he told the guy, “I need to see the king.” The king knew him, it was cool, he was one if his guys. He said, “He’s meditating now. He’s in there, he’s in his chapel. Just go in there and sit in the back, and when he finishes his prayers you can talk to him about whatever you want to talk about.” And then he heard the king ask, “Oh God, give me more riches! Give me more castles! Give me more women! Give me more...” And so he got up to ease out. The king said, “Why are you leaving? What’s going on?” He said, “I

didn’t come here to beg from a beggar,” you know? I mean somehow in there, in the arts, I don’t know why the artists - it’s not so easy to live in your lifetime with your creativity. That’s always saddened me. I’ve been blessed. I’m very blessed.
Oh you are, but you’ve worked so hard.
But I also know not to stick my chest out and to get in front of a Mack truck.
